clue.text: Retired animal and bird writer

indicators.note: a word that has retired has gone back, so the animal is read from end to start

parts.note: a hart is a male deer
the erne is the sea eagle, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A writer who has given up producing books about animals and birds.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Traherne was a seventeenth-century English poet and religious writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Traherne is an example of an English author, known for his poetry and the prose Centuries of Meditations.

clue.text: A bit of a bind for officials when in the red

definitions.text: A bit of a bind for officials when in the red

parts.words: A bit of a bind for officials when in the red
parts.note: surface reading: a nuisance for officials when their accounts are in debt
setter's reading: a strip used for binding, which coloured red is the bureaucracy officials are known for

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the red' suggests being overdrawn; it means coloured red, as in the idiom for bureaucratic delay.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is the idiom for official bureaucracy, from the coloured ribbon once used to tie up legal documents.

clue.text: Breathless greeting to people in the race ground

indicators.note: being breathless means losing the breathy aspirate sound, so the letter for that breath is dropped

parts.note: hallo is a greeting

indicators.note: in says the people are placed inside the race

parts.note: the TT, Tourist Trophy, is the Isle of Man motorcycle race
men are people

explanation.surface: A panting hello to the spectators at the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: An allotment is a small rented plot of land for growing vegetables, common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is a plot of land, so ground here is the noun meaning a piece of earth.

clue.text: Burton settles in comfort in Sussex

definitions.note: the definition is a location phrase; the answer is a town found there

indicators.note: in places the reworked name inside the word for comfort

parts.note: ease is comfort

indicators.note: settling lets things shift into new positions, so the surname's letters are reordered

parts.note: the surname supplies six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The actor Richard Burton makes himself comfortable somewhere in Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: Eastbourne is a seaside resort town on the south coast of England, in the county of East Sussex.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a coastal resort town located in the English county of Sussex, so it lies there.

clue.text: Lane twists round quiet country

indicators.note: round says the twisted word wraps itself around the next piece
twisting distorts something's shape, so the word's letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging
p is the musical marking piano, meaning soft

explanation.surface: A winding road curves around a peaceful rural landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepal is a Himalayan nation between India and China, an example of a sovereign state.

clue.text: Late Dee-side call-girl's charges

parts.note: surface reading: the fees of a dead prostitute who worked by the river Dee
setter's reading: the animals Mary was sent to call home across the sands of Dee in Kingsley's poem

explanation.surface: The fees once charged by a prostitute who worked along the river Dee.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Kingsley's poem The Sands of Dee begins 'O Mary, go and call the cattle home'; Mary drowns, so she is late, and she is the girl told to call.
explanation.definitionFit: Livestock are the charges, meaning creatures in her care, that the drowned girl of the poem was sent to fetch.

clue.text: Girl meets many a gardener

parts.note: Ada is a girl's name
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, hence many

explanation.surface: A girl encounters many a person who tends gardens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'many a gardener' reads as one phrase, but 'many' belongs to the wordplay and 'a gardener' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam tended the Garden of Eden in Genesis, so he is the first and best-known biblical gardener.

clue.text: Letter of some force

parts.note: a particular one, standing for the definite article
the TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: A letter carries some strength or authority.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army was the British army's part-time reserve, so 'the TA' is a force.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet, so it is an example of an alphabetic letter.

clue.text: Heart-breaking labours making fortifications

indicators.note: breaking smashes something into pieces, so the word's letters are put back in another order

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging
works are labours

explanation.surface: Back-breaking toil goes into building defences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart-breaking' looks like the adjective for sad, but the hyphen hides the word to rework and its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthworks are banks and ditches of soil built as defences, a type of military fortification.

clue.text: Not inclined to be languid?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read cryptically: without a list, the lean of a ship, so not tilted
second meaning: lacking energy or interest

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not inclined' suggests unwilling; a ship lists when it leans, so something without a list is not inclined at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means lacking energy or enthusiasm, the same weary state as languid.

clue.text: Hides stones?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: animal skins with the fur on
second meaning: throws missiles at, as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hides' looks like a verb about concealing; here it is the plural noun for skins, while 'stones' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a plural noun for furry animal skins and as a verb for hurling things repeatedly at someone.

clue.text: Soldier about to return by ship

parts.note: a private is the lowest-ranking soldier

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the short word for about is read backwards

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A soldier about to head home on board a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A privateer was a privately owned armed vessel licensed by a government to attack enemy shipping.

clue.text: Shows firmness, in a way, and skill

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
ability is skill or competence

explanation.surface: Someone displays steadiness of character, after a fashion, along with talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' reads like the hedge 'to some extent'; here it supplies the street abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Stability is the quality of being steady and not easily moved, which is what firmness describes.

clue.text: Wood is content to toil at home

indicators.note: the content of something is what sits inside it, so the letters lie within the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of toil, the whole of at and the start of home

explanation.surface: A woodworker is happy to do their labour in their own house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' reads as happy, but it means the contents of the phrase that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A lath is a thin narrow strip of timber, used for example under plaster or in trellis.

clue.text: Put on round a tear, it seems

indicators.note: round says the first word goes around the outside of the next phrase

parts.note: to apply is to put on, as with paint
a rent is a tear in fabric

explanation.surface: Someone puts on clothing around a rip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tear' wants to be the drop from an eye, but it is the rip in cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparently is an adverb meaning as far as one can tell, the same hedge as the phrase it seems.

clue.text: Creature Mr Birch ate by mistake

indicators.note: doing something by mistake gets it wrong, so the letters come out in a garbled order

parts.note: the three words supply all ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A man named Birch accidentally ate some animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface implies he ate it by mistake; the answer is just what he might have eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit crab is a crustacean that lives in an abandoned shell, an example of an animal.

clue.text: Bias connected with pride?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an unfair preconceived opinion
second meaning: the word joined to Pride in the title of Jane Austen's novel

explanation.walkthrough: Jane Austen's novel is Pride and Prejudice, so the word is literally connected with 'Pride' by 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: Prejudice is a judgement formed in advance without fair grounds, which is bias; it is also the second noun of Austen's title.

clue.text: Humoured batting failure about leg-break

parts.note: a cricketer who is batting is in

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the failure wraps around the reworked word

parts.note: a dud is a failure

indicators.note: a break shatters the word's order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator jokes about a batsman's failure against a leg-break delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: A leg-break is a spin bowler's delivery in cricket; the hyphenated word splits into the fodder and its signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To humour someone is to go along with their wishes, so humoured and indulged both mean gratified.

clue.text: Duckweed is retired poet's source of inspiration

indicators.note: something retired has withdrawn backwards, so the combined letters are read in reverse

parts.note: split in two: a duck is a cricket score of nothing, the letter O, and tares are the weeds of the biblical parable

explanation.surface: A retired poet takes inspiration from duckweed, the green scum on ponds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duckweed' looks like one word for the pond plant, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Muse of lyric and love poetry in Greek myth, the goddess a poet invokes for inspiration.

clue.text: Gypsum from a workroom rates as synthetic

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something synthetic is artificially made up, so these letters are constructed into a new word

parts.note: a lab is a laboratory, a scientific workroom
taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: A laboratory judges its gypsum to be man-made.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabaster is a fine-grained white variety of the mineral gypsum, carved for ornaments.

clue.text: A very heavy historian?

parts.note: taken as written
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, and a hundred tons is very heavy indeed

explanation.surface: A query about which historian weighed the most.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the loose idea of a hundred tons standing for something very heavy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Acton was a Victorian historian, remembered for saying that power tends to corrupt.

clue.text: Made brisk repair, as sailor might do

definitions.note: the definition describes the action, a verb phrase, while the answer is the bare verb

indicators.note: to repair is to mend by taking apart and putting back together, so these letters are rebuilt

parts.note: the two words supply all nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone carried out a quick mending job, as a sailor would aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repair' looks like a noun after 'brisk', but it is the verb telling you to rework the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Going ashore from a vessel at the end of a voyage is the typical act of a sailor landing in port.

clue.text: Uniform level

explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like the noun for clothing; here both words are adjectives.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective covers both a steady, unvarying quality and a flat surface with no bumps.

clue.text: First of the Dormouse's three sisters, well in

definitions.text: First of the Dormouse's three sisters, well in

parts.words: First of the Dormouse's three sisters
parts.note: surface reading: the eldest sibling of a dormouse
setter's reading: the first-named of the three girls in the Dormouse's story in Alice in Wonderland, who lived at the bottom of a well

explanation.walkthrough: At the Mad Hatter's tea party the Dormouse tells of three sisters, Elsie, Lacie and Tillie, who lived in a treacle well; 'well in' also sounds like 'well established'.
explanation.definitionFit: She is named first of the three sisters in the Dormouse's tale in Lewis Carroll's Alice book.

clue.text: Fruit tea a penny at Dr Grantly's home in London

parts.note: plums are fruit
taken as written
d was the abbreviation for an old British penny, from the Latin denarius

explanation.surface: A price list offering fruit and tea at a penny each.
explanation.walkthrough: Archdeacon Grantly in Trollope's Barchester novels lives at Plumstead Episcopi; Plumstead is also a district of south-east London.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both the Trollope clergyman's fictional parish and an actual suburb of the British capital.

clue.text: Not drinking in low surroundings — that's the maxim!

indicators.note: in places the abstainer's letters inside the surrounding word

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
TT means teetotal

explanation.surface: Staying sober in a seedy setting is the guiding principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low' looks like an adjective for shabby, but it is the verb for a cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: A motto is a short saying expressing a guiding principle, which is what a maxim is.

clue.text: Something ironically clear about A. Tennyson's work

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word goes around the letter that follows

parts.note: clear as mud is the ironic phrase for something not clear at all
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzle about Alfred Tennyson's writing proves anything but clear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A. Tennyson' looks like the poet's initial, but the A is detached to go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Maud is a long dramatic monologue poem published by Alfred Tennyson in 1855, an example of his work.

clue.text: Pipe or cigar, Henry?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a tobacco pipe made of baked earthenware
second meaning: the Henry ... brand of Cuban cigar
third meaning: the surname of Henry, the American statesman

explanation.walkthrough: Henry Clay was a nineteenth-century American senator, and a famous Havana cigar brand bore his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names an earthenware smoking pipe, a cigar brand and the surname of statesman Henry Clay.

clue.text: Will try to come by morning — ten, roughly

parts.note: to test is to try out

indicators.note: roughly means not precisely, so the letters of the word are only loosely kept in order

parts.note: a.m. means before noon
taken as written before the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone named Will will try to come round in the morning at about ten o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like a person's name or the future tense; it is the legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: A last will and testament is the legal document stating how a person's property is distributed after death.

clue.text: Badger and scold learner

parts.note: to rate is an old word for to scold angrily
L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: Pester and tell off a student.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badger' reads as a verb meaning nag, which suits the surface; it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The ratel is the honey badger, a fierce African and Asian member of the weasel family.

clue.text: Furnishes Disley building

indicators.note: building means constructing, so the place-name's letters are put together into a new structure

parts.note: Disley is a village in Cheshire, used here for its letters

explanation.surface: Supplies the furniture for a building in the village of Disley.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to provide or supply, so yields and furnishes both mean produces for someone.

clue.text: Fruity part in Much Ado

parts.note: surface reading: a juicy or ripe role in a Shakespeare comedy
setter's reading: a character in Much Ado About Nothing whose name is also a wild fruit

explanation.walkthrough: Fruity in theatre slang means rich or saucy; here it means the character's name is literally a berry.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogberry is the bumbling constable in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing, and the dogberry is the fruit of dogwood.
